sermon:
A woman comes back to the town she left, and the people barely know her. They say her name like a question. Is this Naomi? And she stops them in the street and tells them not to use that name anymore. Pleasant is a lie now. Call me Mara. Call me Bitter. The story of Ruth opens not with romance but with a famine, three graves, and a widow who has run out of words for God except hard ones.

It begins in the days when the judges ruled, which is the narrator's way of telling you the floor is rotten before anyone steps on it. Those were the days when everyone did what was right in his own eyes. And there was a famine in Bethlehem, in the house of bread, which is the second thing the narrator wants you to feel. The town named for bread has none. So Elimelech takes his wife and two sons and leaves the land of promise for the fields of Moab, the country of Israel's old enemy. He went to survive. He buried himself there instead.

**Three Funerals and a God Who Does Not Explain**

Elimelech dies. Then the two sons, married now to Moabite women, die also. Ten years pass and the text gives them in a single breath: no sons, no husband, nothing. Naomi is left with two foreign daughters-in-law and a road home. She tells them to go back, to find rest in the houses of new husbands, because she has nothing left to give them. And then she says the thing underneath all of it. The hand of the LORD has gone out against me. She does not say God is absent. She says God is present and against her. That is a harder confession, and a more honest one, than most of us will make in a hard year.

Orpah kisses her and turns back. We should not despise Orpah. She did the reasonable thing. But Ruth clung to her, and out of an empty woman's bitterness came one of the most loyal sentences in all of Scripture: "Intreat me not to leave thee, or to return from following after thee: for whither thou goest, I will go; and where thou lodgest, I will lodge: thy people shall be my people, and thy God my God" (Ruth 1:16). A Moabite widow, with no inheritance and no advantage in it, binds herself to the God who she has just watched take everything from this family. That is not sentiment. That is conversion.

**Bitter, and Still Walking the Right Direction**

Notice where the chapter ends. It does not end with comfort. Naomi arrives still bitter, still naming herself Mara, still convinced the Almighty has emptied her. But the last line says they came to Bethlehem in the beginning of barley harvest. The house of bread has bread again. Naomi cannot see it yet. The reader is meant to.

I am tempted, when a year goes against me, to read God's silence as God's absence, and then to read His absence as His enmity. I have stood where Naomi stood and told people, with my mouth, that the hand of the Lord had gone out against me. The book of Ruth does not scold that grief. It records it without flinching. But it also refuses to let the bitter confession be the whole truth. Naomi says she went out full and came home empty. She is wrong. She came home with Ruth, and Ruth is the thread God is already pulling toward a throne.

This is the road home for the rest of us. We do not always feel the hand that brings us back. We feel the famine, the graves, the long walk with nothing. Yet the same God who let the field go empty has set the barley ripening before we arrive, and has already given us a companion whose loyalty is a small picture of a larger one. There is a Redeemer further down this line who will say to a people with no claim on Him, your people shall be my people. He will leave His own country to bind Himself to widows and foreigners and the bitter. He will be emptied so we are not left in Moab.

Naomi is not abandoned. She only cannot feel the hand yet.

Bitter, but not abandoned.

Two widows are starving, and one of them goes to work. There is no miracle in this chapter. No voice from heaven, no parted sea, no fire. There is a poor woman with a basket, a barley field, and the gleaning law that let the destitute follow the reapers and take what was dropped. Ruth does the most ordinary thing a hungry person can do. She goes out to find food. And the narrator tells us, with a wink we are meant to catch, that "her hap was to light on a part of the field belonging unto Boaz" (Ruth 2:3).

Her hap. By chance. The Hebrew almost shrugs. Of all the fields around Bethlehem, she stumbles into the one owned by a worthy man of Elimelech's clan, a kinsman with the standing to redeem. The text says chance and means the opposite. This is the engine of the whole book. God is not in the thunder here. He is in the accident of the field, the turn at the property line, the day the poor woman picked.

**Kindness Before She Earned It**

Boaz arrives and greets his reapers with the LORD be with you, and they answer the LORD bless thee, and you realize this man's faith has gotten down into his ordinary speech. He notices the stranger. He has already heard about her, how she left her own people and came to a land she did not know to care for her mother-in-law. So before Ruth asks for anything, he gives. He tells her to stay in his field, drink from his vessels, glean among the sheaves, and he charges the young men not to touch her. To a foreign widow with no protector, that protection is everything.

She falls on her face and asks the only honest question. Why have I found grace in thine eyes, seeing I am a stranger? And Boaz answers with the language that holds the chapter together: a full reward be given thee of the LORD God of Israel, under whose wings thou art come to trust. He prays that the God of Israel would cover her. Then he spends the rest of the day being the answer to his own prayer. He feeds her at his table until she is full and leaves some over. He tells the reapers to pull stalks from the bundles on purpose and leave them for her. She gleans an ephah of barley, far more than a day should yield, and carries it home.

**Naming the Hand in the Field**

Naomi sees the haul and asks where she worked, and when she hears the name Boaz, the bitter woman blesses for the first time in the book. Blessed be he of the LORD, who hath not left off his kindness to the living and to the dead. She catches it before Ruth does. The man is one of our near kinsmen. The hand she thought had gone out against her is moving in the barley.

Here is where the chapter searches me. I am quick to call the good things in my life luck and the hard things judgment. I read providence backward. When the field turns out to belong to the right man, I credit timing. When it does not, I credit God's anger. Ruth's hap that was no hap rebukes that whole habit. There is no neutral chance in a world this God governs. The day you stumbled into the right job, the right friend, the marriage you did not engineer, the help that came when you had nothing left to barter, that was not the random kindness of the universe. The universe is not kind. He is.

And Boaz, covering a foreigner under wings that are really God's wings, is a small portrait of a larger Kinsman. There is a Redeemer who heard about us before we ever came near His field, who fed us at a table when we had no claim to a seat, who spread His protection over strangers and widows and told the world not to touch them. Boaz prays that Ruth would find refuge under God's wings. Christ becomes the wings.

Nothing in this field was accident. The poor woman picked, and the hand of God did the choosing.

No such thing as chance.

Naomi has a plan, and it would ruin a lesser woman. She sends Ruth, at night, washed and perfumed, to the threshing floor where Boaz is sleeping by his grain after the harvest celebration. Wait until he lies down, she says. Mark the place. Then go uncover his feet and lie down, and he will tell you what to do. Read that plainly and your stomach should tighten. A widow, a sleeping man, the dark, no witnesses. Everything about the scene could go wrong, and the original readers knew it.

It does not go wrong, and the reason is the heart of the chapter. Two people who could have taken what they wanted from each other instead act in covenant kindness, and God's redemption moves forward on the integrity of ordinary people doing the right thing where no one is watching.

**A Request, Not a Seduction**

Boaz wakes at midnight and is afraid, and there is a woman at his feet. Who art thou? And Ruth answers, and her answer turns the whole night from danger into honor: "I am Ruth thine handmaid: spread therefore thy skirt over thine handmaid; for thou art a near kinsman" (Ruth 3:9). Spread your wing over me. She borrows Boaz's own word from the field, where he had prayed she would find refuge under the wings of the LORD. Now she asks him to be that refuge. Cover me, redeem me, take responsibility for a widow and a dead man's name. It is not a proposal of passion. It is a plea for redemption, made with empty hands.

And Boaz blesses her. He calls this kindness greater than the first. The first kindness was her loyalty to Naomi. This greater one is that she did not run after younger men, rich or poor, but came to the kinsman, seeking to do the costly, lawful thing for her dead husband's house. Then he protects her in the very moment he could have used her. Fear not, he says. I will do all that thou requirest. He guards her purity. He tells her to lie until morning and leave before anyone can recognize her and slander her. The man's restraint is its own sermon.

**The Honest Obstacle**

Then Boaz tells her the truth he could have hidden. It is true that I am thy near kinsman, howbeit there is a kinsman nearer than I. There is a man with a prior claim, and integrity will not let Boaz skip him. He will not seize Ruth by going around the law. He pledges to settle it in the morning, in the open, at the gate, the right way or not at all. He sends her home with six measures of barley so she does not return to Naomi empty, and Naomi, reading the man, tells her to sit still, for he will not rest until he has finished the thing this day.

This chapter exposes how rarely I do the right thing when the wrong thing is available and unseen. The threshing floor is the room with no witnesses, and most of us are more honest in the daylight than in the dark. Boaz had Ruth at his feet, an advantage no one would have questioned, and he chose covenant over advantage, and he chose the harder lawful path over the easier private one. I want to be that man, and I have failed to be, in smaller rooms than that one.

But look at what Ruth models, because this is the gospel turned toward us. She comes with nothing to offer and asks to be covered. She does not earn the redeemer's wing by her merit. She asks for it, lays herself at his feet, and trusts his kindness to do what she cannot do for herself. That is exactly how a sinner comes to Christ. Not bargaining. Not impressing. Lying down at the Redeemer's feet and asking Him to spread His covering over us, because He has the right and we have only the need.

Boaz will not rest until it is finished. Neither did the One who came after him.

Redemption sought with empty hands.

Redemption finally happens in public, in daylight, at the city gate, in front of ten elders and a crowd. After the secrecy of the threshing floor, the narrator pulls everything into the open, because real redemption is not a private feeling. It is a transaction. Someone owes. Someone pays. And the whole town watches who is willing.

Boaz goes up to the gate, the place where business and justice were done, and sits down. The nearer kinsman comes by, and Boaz hails him, and gathers ten elders as witnesses, and lays the matter out. Naomi is selling the parcel of land that belonged to Elimelech. You are first in line to redeem it. Will you buy it back and keep it in the family? And the man says yes immediately, because a field is an asset. I will redeem it. Of course he will. Land is gain.

**The Cost He Would Not Pay**

Then Boaz adds the part that changes the arithmetic. What day thou buyest the field of the hand of Naomi, thou must buy it also of Ruth the Moabitess, the wife of the dead, to raise up the name of the dead upon his inheritance. The field comes with a widow, and the widow comes with an obligation. Any son born would carry the dead man's name and inherit the land you just bought, so you spend on it and gain nothing lasting for your own house. And the kinsman backs out at once. I cannot redeem it, lest I mar mine own inheritance. Redeem thou it; for I cannot redeem it.

There is the whole difference between the two men. Both had the right. Only one had the willingness. The nearer kinsman wanted the part of redemption that profited him and refused the part that cost him. He is not a villain. He is most of us. We will redeem what adds to our inheritance and decline what threatens it. Boaz takes the widow and the obligation and the loss, and counts it worth doing. He says it plainly before the elders: "Moreover Ruth the Moabitess, the wife of Mahlon, have I purchased to be my wife, to raise up the name of the dead upon his inheritance, that the name of the dead be not cut off from among his brethren, and from the gate of his place: ye are witnesses this day" (Ruth 4:10).

**The Name He Bought Back**

Hear what he is paying for. Not a profit. A name. The name of a dead man who can never thank him, a foreign woman's first husband, a household that the world would have let vanish without noticing. Boaz spends his own inheritance so that someone else's name will not be cut off. The crowd blesses him and the elders bless him, and they pray that his house would be built like the house of Pharez, with a reference that lands oddly until you remember the genealogy that is coming. They are blessing a line they cannot see the end of.

This gate exposes a calculation I run more than I admit. I love redemption in the abstract and shrink from it when it touches my inheritance, my time, my reputation, my margin. I will help the person whose need does not cost me much. I have stood in the place of the nearer kinsman, saying the polite version of I cannot redeem it, lest I mar mine own. The willing redeemer is the rarer man, and he is rare because love that pays the full cost is rare.

Which is why Boaz at the gate is the clearest portrait in the book of the One he points to. There was a Redeemer who had every right to keep His inheritance and decline ours, who looked at a people with nothing to offer and a name about to be cut off forever, and who said before heaven and earth, I have purchased them to be mine. He paid not in silver at a gate but in blood at a cross, and He bought back a name for the dead. He took the part of redemption that cost Him everything, and counted us worth it.

The nearer kinsman kept his inheritance. Boaz spent his. So did Christ.

Love that pays the cost.

The book ends with a baby and a list of names, and you could read right past the second one. But the genealogy is the point the whole story has been climbing toward. A famine, three graves, a bitter widow, a foreign gleaner, a redeemer at the gate, and it all turns out to have been God quietly writing a king.

Boaz takes Ruth, and the LORD gives her conception, and she bears a son. Notice who gets the credit. Not the marriage, not biology, the LORD gave. The same God who let the field go empty in chapter one fills the womb in chapter four, and the narrator wants His hand named at the birth as plainly as Naomi named it at the loss. She said the Almighty had emptied her. The text answers her, slowly, across four chapters, and now it answers her completely.

**The Women Bless the Emptied Woman**

The women of Bethlehem, the same town that once whispered is this Naomi, now gather around her and bless God. "Blessed be the LORD, which hath not left thee this day without a kinsman, that his name may be famous in Israel. And he shall be unto thee a restorer of thy life, and a nourisher of thine old age: for thy daughter in law, which loveth thee, which is better to thee than seven sons, hath born him" (Ruth 4:14-15). Hear what they undo. Naomi came home saying she was empty, that she had nothing, that the hand of the Lord was against her. The women hand her a child and tell her the foreign daughter-in-law she once tried to send back to Moab is worth more to her than seven sons. In a culture that counted seven sons as the fullness of blessing, a Moabite widow is reckoned higher. Naomi takes the child and lays him in her bosom, and the woman who renamed herself Bitter holds her redemption in her lap.

The neighbor women name him. There is a son born to Naomi. They call his name Obed.

**The Hidden Hand Revealed**

Then comes the line that re-reads everything. Obed is the father of Jesse, and Jesse is the father of David. The hidden Moabite widow, the gleaner in a stranger's field, the woman with no claim and no future, becomes the great-grandmother of Israel's greatest king. Every chance that was no chance, every ordinary loyalty, every costly act of redemption at a gate, was God laying track toward the throne. No one in the story could see it. Naomi could not see it when she walked home empty. Ruth could not see it gleaning barley. Boaz could not see the whole line he was blessing. The reader sees it only on the last page, and only because God let us.

This is the comfort I keep needing and keep failing to hold onto. I judge my life by the chapter I am standing in. When the field is empty, I conclude the story is empty. When the year is loss and graves and the long walk home, I name God's hand as the hand against me, and I mean it the way Naomi meant it. The genealogy is God's reply to that despair. The years that looked like nothing were the years He was building a king. He does not always tell us in the chapter. He tells us at the end, and He asks us to trust the pattern before we reach it.

And the list does not stop at David, because the New Testament picks it up. Matthew opens his Gospel with these same names, Boaz and Obed and Jesse and David, and runs the line forward to Jesus. The Redeemer at the gate stands at the head of a line that reaches the Redeemer at the cross. The God who gathered a foreigner and a widow into the family of the king was, the whole time, gathering foreigners and widows into the family of Christ. Ruth's empty hands held the future. So do ours, if His hand is the one filling them.

The years looked like nothing. God was writing a king.

God was writing a king.
